description: Somos Hertz Hunters, un equipo salvadoreño que ama crear juegos y herramientas interactivas. Vamos por el reto Earth Information Jukebox: convertir visualizaciones de la Tierra de la NASA en sonido para que todos, incluidas personas ciegas o con baja visión, puedan sentir cómo cambia nuestro planeta. Sabemos de gamificación, visión por computadora y desarrollo web. Creemos en ayudarnos y aprender juntos. Buscamos gente de música/audio y diseño UI/UX o accesibilidad. ¡Únete a la cacería!
summary: Earthbeat is an accessible web "jukebox" that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into sound, so people who are blind or have low vision can experience how our planet changes. For four NASA Scientific Visualization Studio datasets — ocean currents and temperature, night lights, aerosols, and forest canopy height — we read the source imagery, convert color into real physical values, and play a synchronized sound scene in the browser. Pitch, rhythm, texture and instrumentation follow the data: warmer water sounds higher, with audible "foam" past 27 °C; a radar line sweeps the night-lights map; each aerosol type gets its own instrument. Our rule is "emotion follows the data" — musical, but faithful. The app is accessibility-first: full keyboard control, screen-reader announcements, skip links, high-contrast and reduced-motion modes, and an "About the track" panel with data provenance and interpretation limits. It matters because climate information should not be visual-only — Earthbeat lets everyone feel the planet's rhythms.
details:
WHAT IT IS / HOW IT WORKS

Earthbeat is an accessible web "jukebox" that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into sound. The user opens the Collection, picks one of four tracks, reads an "About the track" panel (period, variable, source, and interpretation limits), and plays a sound scene synchronized with the NASA source image: a listening line sweeps the map while the sonification plays. The pipeline is image → value → sound — we read the NASA source imagery, convert each color into its real physical value using the official colorbars, and map those values to audio (pitch, rhythm, texture, instrument). A footer player (play, progress, volume) drives the Tone.js sound engine.

THE FOUR TRACKS (all NASA Scientific Visualization Studio data)

• Ocean currents & temperature (SVS 3912, ECCO2): warmer water = higher pitch; audible "foam" above 27 °C.

• Night lights (Black Marble, SVS 5276/5313): a radar line sweeps the globe; where there is light, a piano plays.

• Aerosols (SVS 5669): one instrument per particle type (dust, sea salt, sulfate, black carbon).

• Forest canopy height (GEDI, SVS 4950): the piano "climbs the tree," point by point.

BENEFITS & IMPACT

Climate information is communicated almost entirely through images and video, which excludes people who are blind or have low vision and limits how the public connects with the science. Earthbeat makes the same NASA data perceivable through hearing, giving everyone a more emotional, memorable way to experience how our planet is changing.

TOOLS & TECHNOLOGY

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite. Audio: Web Audio API + Tone.js, with piano samples loaded at runtime. Data pipeline: Python with Pillow and FFmpeg (scripts/sonify.py) to read the imagery, extract values and generate audio. 3D welcome globe: a WebGL mesh using Natural Earth cartography and GEDI canopy-height data (WGS84). Accessibility: Atkinson Hyperlegible typeface, high-contrast and reduced-motion modes, ARIA live regions, keyboard navigation and skip links. Designed in Figma, deployed on GitHub Pages, and runs with no API keys.

CREATIVITY

Instead of mapping pixels directly (which produces chaotic noise), we designed artistic rules per dataset using musical scales, thresholds and harmonies, guided by one principle: "emotion follows the data" — if the data does not change, the sound does not change. A pixel-art "disc/jukebox" aesthetic keeps the experience playful while the science stays honest.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility first (not an add-on); a balance between data fidelity and musicality; transparency about each dataset's limits (one-year model, averaged maps, approximate heights); serving all assets locally to avoid CORS issues; and keeping the app lightweight and key-free so anyone can run it.

We used AI tools as assistants; all scientific data comes from NASA and all final decisions were made by our team.

• AI coding assistants (Claude / Claude Code and OpenAI Codex) helped us write and refactor the React/TypeScript app, the accessibility features and the image-to-sound pipeline, and supported documentation and English translation.

• We used AI for brainstorming and copywriting support.

• For the demo video, we used ElevenLabs text-to-speech to generate the narrator's voice.

No scientific data or imagery was generated by AI — every dataset comes from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio / Earth Information Center. The sonification rules, artistic mapping, code review and creative direction were decided and verified by our team.
